content: Three new HIV vaccines are currently under investigation: Ad4-Env150KN, Ad4-Env145NFL, and VRC-HIVRGP096-00-VP (Trimer 4571). These vaccines are being evaluated in clinical trials to determine their safety and efficacy in preventing HIV infection. Adjuvants such as aluminum hydroxide fluid gel (AHFG), Army Liposomal Formulation (ALFQ), and glucopyranosyl lipid adjuvant-stable emulsion (GLA-SE) are being used to enhance immune responses in these vaccine formulations. Broadly neutralizing antibodies (bNAbs) like PGDM1400, VRC07-523LS, and PGT121 are being tested for their ability to prevent HIV infection. These antibodies are administered via intravenous infusion or subcutaneous injection, either alone or in combination, to evaluate their protective effects. Long-acting antiretroviral (ARV) agents, such as islatravir, cabotegravir, and lenacapavir, are being developed for HIV prevention. Islatravir is being studied as a once-monthly oral dose and as an annual subdermal implant. Cabotegravir is administered as an oral tablet for one month, followed by intramuscular injections every eight weeks. Lenacapavir is being tested as a twice-yearly subcutaneous injection. Vaginal rings containing antiretroviral drugs like dapivirine and levonorgestrel are being explored as sustained-release options for HIV prevention in women. These rings are designed to provide protection for up to three months. Non-antiretroviral-based microbicides, such as gels containing griffithsin and carrageenan, are also being investigated for their potential to prevent HIV, human papillomavirus (HPV), and herpes simplex virus (HSV) infections. The use of pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) with tenofovir-based regimens has shown significant efficacy in preventing HIV infection in various populations, including men who have sex with men, heterosexual men and women, and transgender individuals. Studies have demonstrated the importance of adherence to PrEP regimens to maximize their protective effects. The development of long-acting injectable formulations, such as cabotegravir, has shown promise in providing highly effective HIV prevention, particularly in populations at high risk of infection. These formulations offer an alternative to daily oral PrEP, addressing challenges related to adherence. The dapivirine vaginal ring has been approved by the European Medicines Agency (EMA) for use in women in high HIV burden settings. The World Health Organization (WHO) has also recommended the dapivirine ring as a new prevention option for women at substantial risk of HIV infection. Efforts to scale up HIV vaccine research and the development of innovative prevention technologies are critical to achieving a sustainable end to the AIDS epidemic. These advancements aim to address the global burden of HIV and improve access to effective prevention strategies for diverse populations.
